subject: operating-systems
title: System-call lifecycle and error handling
summary: A wrapper passes an operation and arguments through a controlled entry mechanism; the kernel validates the request and returns a result or error.

resources.title: syscall(2): Invoke a system call
resources.why: Describes syscall arguments, return values, and errno behavior.

resources.title: syscalls(2): Linux system calls
resources.why: Lists system calls and explains their role as the application-to-kernel interface.

questions.prompt: For many Linux C-library wrappers, how is a system-call failure commonly reported?
options: Return -1 and set errno
Retry forever until success
Return a positive process ID and clear errno
Return 0 and overwrite every buffer
questions.answerKey: Many glibc wrappers report failure as -1 and set errno to describe the error; exact return conventions depend on the call.
questions.explanation: Do not generalize one return convention to every system call.

questions.prompt: Why must a kernel validate pointers and permissions supplied with a system-call request?
options: Compiled programs cannot contain invalid pointers
User input can be invalid or unauthorized, and the kernel must not trust it blindly
A mode switch makes every pointer valid
Validation is only needed when the system has no files
questions.answerKey: System-call arguments cross a protection boundary and must be checked before the kernel uses them or performs privileged work.
questions.explanation: Privilege transition does not make arbitrary user data trustworthy.

questions.prompt: A process calls open("secret.txt", O_RDONLY), but file permissions deny read access. What should the OS do?
options: Delete the file
Open the file because O_RDONLY overrides permissions
Switch the process permanently to kernel mode
Fail the request and report an access error
questions.answerKey: The OS checks permissions; O_RDONLY chooses the requested access mode but does not bypass access controls.
questions.explanation: Access mode and authorization are separate checks.

questions.prompt: A Linux wrapper returns -1 and sets errno to EACCES after open(). Which interpretation is best?
options: The request failed because access was denied; the caller should handle the error path
The process must always terminate immediately
The file opened successfully with descriptor -1
The kernel necessarily panicked
questions.answerKey: EACCES indicates a permission/access failure in this context; application behavior after failure is a design choice.
questions.explanation: A system-call failure does not itself imply a kernel crash or mandatory process termination.

questions.prompt: A kernel handler dereferences a user-provided pointer without safely checking or copying the referenced data. What is the principal risk?
options: The pointer is automatically replaced with errno
The pointer automatically becomes a safe kernel pointer
Invalid user memory can cause faults or unsafe kernel behavior
The call is guaranteed to be faster and correct
questions.answerKey: Kernel code must safely access user memory; an arbitrary user pointer cannot be trusted just because execution entered kernel mode.
questions.explanation: Mode transition does not validate the pointer for the kernel.

questions.prompt: Describe the typical path from a C library system-call wrapper to the result returned to the application. Include validation and failure reporting.
questions.answerKey: The wrapper prepares the system-call identifier and arguments and invokes the architecture's controlled entry mechanism. The kernel handler validates arguments and permissions, performs or rejects the request, and returns a result. For many Linux C-library interfaces, the wrapper translates an error into -1 and sets errno; exact details depend on the interface and architecture.

rubric.criterion: Kernel validation and service or rejection

questions.explanation: The answer must include ordered control flow, validation, and the caller-visible error convention.
